units.translation: And you will know both the just and the untimely keeper of the city among the citizens.
You will know, taught late at least, to be wise.
You will know, being old, that learning is hard.
But since you think to do and say these things, you will know soon.
And he will know the words in time.
Those things I knew.
A bad prophet indeed would know these things.
Know the insolence of men.
Know not to revere human things too much.
But you yourself know how to pilot the city.
But you yourself now know whom you think to send.
No banishment for blood, decided by the vote of the city,
I know
I become
I have known

having been decided
you will know
you will know
not condemned for any blood by a public vote of the city driving us out
Glaukos
Glaukos Pontios and Glaukos Potnieus were the titles of Aeschylus' plays (fr. 23-39).
Glaukos of the Sea
Glaukos of Potniai
sweet
sweet, pleasant
Do not care for me more than is sweet to me.
For the sick it is sweet to know clearly the pain that remains.
And a sweet life without lamentations.
tongue
tongue
Of the tongue which is in the mouth
in a proverbial expression, on which see under βοῦς [ox].

where the sense requires the opposite: προφθάσασα καρδίαν γλῶσσα πάντ᾽ ἂν ἐξέχει [the tongue, anticipating the heart, would pour out everything], which Schuetz conjectured, with others objecting in vain.
Much more frequently of the tongue insofar as we use it in speaking and of speech itself.

where the neglected position is to be noted: for οὐδ᾽ ἔτι [no longer] is a dactyl, so that dé before γλῶσσαν [tongue] is shortened in the trimeter Ag. 1629. and κέντημα γλώσσης [sting of the tongue] fr. 165, where Lobeck on Soph. Ai. 60 p. 103 conjectured κέντημα λύσσης [sting of madness].
i.e. not from what is said, but from the thing itself. See similar examples in Thes. vol. 2 p. 659.

for the sake of talking, i.e. μὴ δυνάμενος ἐχεμυθεῖν [not being able to keep silent], as the scholiast explains. Similarly Hesiod Op. 707 μηδὲ ψεύδεσθαι γλώσσης χάριν [nor to lie for the sake of the tongue], which Proclus interprets as διὰ περιττὴν καὶ ἀνόνητον γλώττης ὁρμήν [through excessive and useless impulse of the tongue].
|| Of tongue, i.e. speech proper to a people
Of dialect
Thus Thucydides 3, 112 said γλῶσσαν Δωρίδα ἱέναι [to speak the Doric tongue].
A sting of the tongue, a scorpion's dart.
A great ox has stepped upon my tongue.
The tongue, anticipating the heart, would pour out these things.
The tongue of a hateful dog (i.e. Clytaemnestra), licking (thus Tyrwhitt for λέξασα) and stretching out with bright mind.
But there is also for me a key as guard upon my tongue.
A tongue shooting not the vital parts.
Your tongue speaks things similar in form.
Of the tongue too lofty-speaking.
By a vain tongue loss is incurred.
Unrestrained of tongue.
The tongue told tales.
For in cowardice fear seizes the tongue.
The tongue becomes a true accuser.
Who will not allow the tongue, flowing without deeds inside the gates, to nourish evils.
No longer is the tongue in guard for mortals.
It is not fitting to defile a day of good omen with a tongue bearing evil tidings.
Guiding the tongue in fortune.
